E032-01.notes: Date in an introductory phrase needs a comma between day and year and after the year: 'On December 21, 1913, the New York World printed...'. A lacks the day/year comma; C lacks the closing comma; D has neither.

E032-02.notes: Register/tone: only 'eagerly took up' fits the formal informational style; A, B, D are slang. C also works grammatically with 'the new feature'.

E032-03.notes: With neither...nor, the verb agrees with the nearer subject, 'Wynne' (singular): 'was prepared'. A, B, C are plural forms; B and C also mismatch tense.

E032-04.notes: The current sentence sets up the time contrast with 'Then, in 1924...' and leads into the book. 'About a decade' (1913 to 1924) is accurate. B, C, D are off topic or out of chronological order.

E032-05.notes: Only B gives specific evidence of sales (sold out its first printing, reprinted repeatedly). This matches the history of the 1924 Simon & Schuster crossword book. C and D are vague.

E032-06.notes: The plural decade is '1920s' with no apostrophe and no possessive here. A uses the apostrophe form the ACT treats as wrong; B and D are possessive forms.

E032-07.notes: 'People' is already plural, so its possessive is 'people's'. A ('peoples'') would mean multiple ethnic peoples; B has no possessive; C is malformed.

E032-08.notes: Editorials suggest, or imply, things; readers infer them. 'Imposed' makes no sense; 'inferring' is ungrammatical after 'that'. The historical claim that the Times ran editorials mocking the fad is accurate.

E032-09.notes: The sentence contrasts with the critics in the previous paragraph (the fad lasted despite them), so 'Still' fits. 'Indeed', 'Likewise' and 'Accordingly' all wrongly signal agreement or a result.

E032-10.notes: 'The paper's editors' and 'in wartime' refer to the Times starting its crossword in 1942 (Sentence 2) and explain that decision. Placing it after 3 or 4 breaks the link. The facts (1942 start, wartime-distraction rationale, Farrar as first editor) are accurate.
